More translational warranted to facilitate microbiome-based personalized therapy. etabolizing enzymes · Drug transporters Introduction The gut microbiota are microorganisms that inhabit the gastrointestinal tract and are composed of various species of yeast, viruses, and bacteria.

Among them, bacteria are the most predominant species in the human colon, with 1 011–1012 cells/g of intestinal content, accounting for approximately 60% of fecal solids (Simon and Gorbach 1984; Guarner and Malagelada 20.

Although the gut microbiota composition is extremely diverse, 90% of the gut microbiota consists of Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes (Arumugam et al. The Firmicutes phylum, which is gram-positive and has a rigid cell wall structure, includes Bacillus, Lactobacillus, Clostridiales, and Enterococcus, whereas Bacteroidetes are gram-negative, and Bacteroides, Alistipes, and Parabacteroides are the most dominant genera in this phylum (Gibiino et al. The Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio is associated with several pathophysiological conditions, such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), prostate enlargement, and metabolic disease (Stojanov et al. 2020; Takezawa et al. 2021; Yañez et al. Vol.:(0112 334567 Considering that the collective human microbiome has 3.3 million genes, which is 150 times more than human genes (Zhu et al. 20, it is important to thoroughly investigate the roles of the microbiota in humans.

By residing in the gastrointestinal tract, the gut microbiota is responsible for the breakdown of some dietary fiber that humans cannot digest because of the lack of the appropriate enzymes (Valdes et al. Modifying endogenous materials, such as bile acids, and preventing infections by exogenous factors are also critical roles of the gut microbiota.
More importantly, the association with human health has recently become the most significant role of the gut microbiota.

Clinically significant associations between gut microbiota and several diseases, such as IBD, Parkinson’s disease, cardiovascular disease, and cancer, have been suggested (Nishida et al. 2018; Wong and Yu 2019; Chen et al. Thus, understanding the gut microbiota is expected to be a continuous subject of interest in investigations to improve human health.

Pharmacomicrobiomics, which has recently emerged as a new strategy for personalized medicine, has been used to investigate the influence of microbial variability on drug pharmacokinetics, efficacy, and safety (Doestzada et al. Although this term was initiated in 2010, the first recognition of the role of gut microbiota in drug efficacy via pharmacokinetic modulation was reported in the 1930s for sulfa antibiotics (Mani et al. Nevertheless, the potential for the involvement of gut microbiota in drug pharmacokinetics was considered unlikely in the past.
It was widely recognized that drugs cannot reach the gut microbiota because most drugs are absorbed before entering the colon that the gut microbiota exist.

However, formulations of drugs that delay drug release for prolonged efficacy or research showing the existence of gut microbiota in the small intestine have changed the paradigm for the concept, accelerating investigations on the roles of gut microbiota in pharmacotherapy (El Aidy et al. In addition, the gut microbiota produce diverse metabolites that are absorbed across the intestinal membrane and are then be exposed to the whole body through the systemic circulation.

The metabolites in tissues can modify the expression of genes that critically affect drug pharmacokinetics, such as drugmetabolizing enzymes or transporters, subsequently altering drug efficacy or safety profiles.
Hence, investigations into the roles of the gut microbiota in drug pharmacokinetics are crucial for optimizing therapy to meet the intended treatment goal.

In this paper, we review the influence of gut microbiota on drug pharmacokinetics, primarily based on drug metabolism and transporters, which are the most critical factors in the movement of drugs after administration.

In particular, we focus on the underlying mechanisms of their associations to facilitate translational research to integrate clinical Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 53:73–92 studies with in vitro/pre-clinical studies, which will provide critical information for the advancement of the utilization of microbiome-based personalized therapy in clinical settings.

Inter‑individual variability of gut microbiota The Human Microbiome Project, intended to identify and characterize the human microbiota to expand our understanding of its association with human health and disease, demonstrated that bacteria are much more variable than expected.
Variations in the gut microbiota may induce different drug pharmacokinetics and alter drug efficacy and safety.
Several conditions have been reported to alter the composition or structure of the gut microbiome.

The development of gut microbiota in the early phase of life may be affected by diverse factors such as microbial transfer during pregnancy, intake of antibiotics, or exposure to external microbes (Penders et al. 2006; Adlerberth et al. While the status of the gut microbiota developed in the early period is crucial for host tolerance to disease risk or response to external stimuli, many other factors also affect the condition and types of the gut microbiota throughout a lifetime after the development period.
Diet has a significant impact on the composition, diversity, and metabolic functions of gut microbiota.
In a study by David et al. (20, subjects with an animal-based diet showed an increase in bile-tolerant microbes, and a possible link between microbes and IBD was suggested.
Yun et al. (20 also reported that diet is a strong covariate in determining gut microbial richness and diversity in diet intervention mice model.

Accordingly, multiple studies have been conducted to modify the gut microbiota to improve host health outcomes and reduce disease risk based on dietary intervention (Healey et al. Drugs or supplemental medicines can alter the condition of gut microbiota.

For example, atorvastatin and rosuvastatin significantly increased the levels of Bacteroides, Butyricimonas, and Mucispirillum, which are associated with an inflammatory response in mice (Kim et al. The administration of simvastatin in rats fed a high-fat diet altered the metabolic pathways of amino acids and fatty acids, along with the modified existence of Ruminococcaceae and Lactobacillus, suggesting an association between drugs taken for disease treatment and gut microbiota.

Besides, in the project with more than 2000 subjects with varying degrees of metabolic and cardiovascular disease, it was found that obesity-associated microbiota dysbiosis is negatively associated with statin treatment (Vieira-Silva et al. 20, suggesting the crucial association between drugs and gut microbiota.

Conditions within the gastrointestinal tract (i.e., pH and bile salt content) also affect bacterial populations (Lkhagva et al. Drugs may be metabolized by the gut microbiota inhabiting the gastrointestinal tract.

The metabolites formed from drugs, diet, or endogenous substances by the gut microbiota may alter the expressional levels of drug-metabolizing enzymes Associations between disease and gut microbiota have also been widely reported.
Imbalance of gut microbiota is associated with gastrointestinal conditions such as IBD or metabolic disease including type 2 diabetes (Bull and Plummer 20.

However, their relationship needs to be clarified further to determine whether disease induces discrepancies in the condition of the gut microbiota or whether the gut microbiota itself is a provoking factor for disease (Durack and Lynch 20.

Other factors, including genetics, environmental exposure, and aging, are also known to induce interindividual variability in the gut microbiome (Lázár et al. As reviewed in the following sections, the inter-individual variability of the gut microbiome induced by several factors may result in pharmacokinetic alterations of drugs through various mechanisms.
Altered drug metabolisms by gut microbiota Drug metabolism is a critical factor contributing to the pharmacokinetic profiles of drugs and consequently affects drug efficacy or safety profiles.
Continuous publications, especially for unexpected toxicity associated with altered drug concentrations by drug interactions or genetic or transporters.

In addition, the metabolites may compete for the metabolizing enzymes or transporters with drugs subsequently altering drug pharmacokinetics accompanied by unexpected toxicity or treatment failure polymorphisms, highlight the importance of maintaining proper drug concentrations within the body (Grenader et al. 2007; Cadeddu et al. 2015; Chae et al. Altered drug metabolism by the gut microbiota is an emerging factor for pharmacokinetic changes (Crouwel et al. 2021; Bai et al. 20, and research on the association between gut microbiota and drug metabolism may provide clues for unexplainable pharmacokinetic changes.

Here, we review the cases of altered drug metabolism caused by the gut microbiota through the use of metabolic activity, alteration of host drugmetabolizing enzyme expression, or production of microbial metabolites competing for host drug-metabolizing enzymes (Fig. The gut microbiota directly metabolize drugs A variety of studies have shown that gut microbiota can metabolize drugs or other compounds by utilizing their enzymatic activity (Table 1).

The metabolism by gut microbiota occurs mainly via reduction or hydrolysis reactions, which is distinctive from humans, where oxidation and conjugation reactions are the metabolic pathways in most cases (Xie et al. The reductase activity of the gut microbiota presents broad substrate specificity, with diverse reaction ranges for drugs (Koppel et al. The hydrolytic activity of gut microbiota breaks down large molecules into smaller ones using hydrolase enzymes such as β-glucosidase or β-glucuronidase (Kim and Kobashi 1986; Noh et al. Transferase activity of gut microbiota to translocate functional groups, such as acyl or methyl groups, via nucleophilic substitution reactions is also responsible for drug metabolism (Kumano et al. The types of metabolic process in gut microbiota may be overlapped with the ones in humans, however, substrate specificity of relevant enzymes and dominant process in overall drug metabolism are distinctive between gut microbiota and humans.
The earliest experimental evidence for drug metabolism by gut microbiota was provided in the case of prontosil and neoprontosil.
Prontosil and neoprontosil do not present antibacterial activity; however, they become effective when reduced to sulfanilamide.

Gingell et al. (19 observed that urinary excretion of sulfanilamide decreased after oral administration of prontosil or neoprontosil in rats pretreated with antibiotics, suggesting the involvement of gut microbiota in the reduction process of the drug.

In addition, they also showed that incubation of prontosil or neoprontosil in feces or cecal contents collected from the rats pretreated with antibiotics decreased the reduction to sulfanilamide, verifying the roles of gut microbiota in drug metabolism.

Similar to the mechanism of prontosil and neoprontosil, prodrugs of 5-aminosalicylate are reduced by azoreductase of gut microbiota existing in the human gastrointestinal tract. 5-aminosalicylate is a biologically active compound that effectively treats ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease (Klotz 19.

Because of its highly permeable properties in the upper jejunum before reaching the colon, which is the target therapeutic site of the drug, prodrugs of 5-aminosalicylate, such as sulfasalazine, balsalazide, and olsalazine, which release free 5-aminosalicylate in the colon by gut microbiota, are widely used for the treatment of IBD (Bhattacharya and Cross 20.
Thus, for the optimal treatment effect for the prodrugs of 5-aminosalicylate in IBD patients, maintenance of a well-controlled composition and condition of the gut microbiota is necessary.

The intake of probiotic bacteria (Lactobacillus acidophilus, Bifidobacterium lactis, and Lactobacillus rhamnosus) has been shown to increase the azoreductase activity of colon contents in rats (Lee et al. 20, and the use of probiotics in patients may be one of the strategies to enhance treatment efficiency.
Digoxin is a well-known example of a critical association between the microbial metabolism of drugs and their efficacy.
Digoxin, a pharmacologically active ingredient Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 53:73–92 isolated from Digitalis purpureaplant, is indicated to treat heart failure or atrial fibrillation.

Therapeutic drug monitoring is essential for patients taking digoxin to maintain consistent ranges of systemic concentration (Grześk et al. 20 because of its narrow therapeutic range and the factors affecting the pharmacokinetic profiles of the drug can change the treatment effect or induce fatal toxicity.

In an early study, it was observed that digoxin is reduced by the gut microbiota, namely Eggerthella lenta (Dobkin et al. 19, and afterward, the cardiac glycoside reductase (cgr) operon of E. lenta is responsible for digoxin reduction.

High inter-individual variability in pharmacokinetics and efficacy can partially be attributed to E. lenta because only some patients possess these bacteria, resulting in reduced systemic exposure (Haiser et al. In these patients, concomitant administration of antibiotics can inhibit the microbial metabolic process of digoxin, thereby increasing its systemic concentrations, as shown by several clinical studies (Rengelshausen et al. 2003; Mezaal et al. Critical interactions for digoxin may also occur with diet such as a highprotein intake.

Arginine, a general amino acid, is known to decrease digoxin metabolism by reducing the expression of cgr in an in vitro study (Haiser et al. This relationship with pharmacokinetic results was also proven in a study that showed increased serum or urinary concentrations of digoxin in mice administered a high-protein diet (Haiser et al. Collectively, diverse factors affecting microbial metabolism of digoxin must be controlled to avoid unexpected toxic events and meet the intended therapeutic efficacy.

The enterohepatic circulation of drugs or their metabolites, which shows movement from the liver to the intestine and back to the liver, can partly be attributed to the β-glucuronidase activity of the gut microbiota.
Some glucuronidated drugs are excreted via bile and can encounter the gut microbiota in the intestine, which presents β-glucuronidase activity.

Although glucuronidated compounds do not easily permeate the intestinal membrane, deglucuronidated forms are prone to be absorbed again across the membrane because of the decrease in size and hydrophilicity.

SN-38, the active metabolite of irinotecan indicated for some types of cancer, such as colon cancer and small cell lung cancer, is a representative case of enterohepatic circulation because of the gut microbiota.
After irinotecan is hydrolyzed to SN-38 followed by glucuronidation, SN-38 glucuronide (SN-38G) is excreted into the intestine via biliary transport.

Free SN-38 is then regenerated by gut microbiota (Takakura et al. 20, placing it in direct contact with the intestinal tract, inducing gastrointestinal toxicity (Mathijssen et al. Thus, the activity of β-glucuronidase plays an important role in inter-individual variable toxicity of irinotecan.

This concept is supported by several studies showing decreased irinotecan-induced intestinal toxicity by the co-administration of β-glucuronidase inhibitors (Cheng Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 53:73–92 et al. 2019; Bhatt et al. 2020; Yue et al. Accordingly, β-glucuronidase activity has been suggested as a biomarker for predicting the severity of diarrhea in patients taking irinotecan (Chamseddine et al. This approach will aid in selecting an optimal therapeutic regimen for each patient with reduced toxicity while retaining efficacy.
The involvement of gut microbiota in direct drug metabolism has been reported for statins.

Incubation of statins, such as atorvastatin, fluvastatin, or simvastatin, with human feces induces drug degradation (Zhao et al. The metabolic process of simvastatin by gut microbiota is well characterized and involves demethylation, hydroxylation, dehydroxylation, and β-oxidation, based on metabolomic studies (Aura et al. In the case of lovastatin, the potential involvement of the gut microbiota in the conversion of lovastatin to β-hydroxy acid lovastatin, which is an active form, has been suggested in earlier studies (Yoo et al. 2014; Nkamga et al. However, later it was demonstrated that the conversion process occurs spontaneously in neutral and basic conditions, although it is gut microbiota-independent, with the result showing the degradation of lovastatin into the β-hydroxy acid form in the absence of gut microbiota (Beltrán et al. Thus, additional careful attention may be needed to evaluate the involvement of the gut microbiota in the drug metabolism process.

Drugs, such as calcitonin, insulin, nitrazepam, nizatidine, and zonisamide, are directly metabolized by the gut microbiota (Takeno 1991; Kitamura et al. 1997; Tozaki et al. 1997; Basit et al. Although many more drugs are suggested to be metabolized by the gut microbiota, experimental evidence is still limited to prove direct metabolism for some drugs; thus, further study is necessary to support this mechanism.
In addition to therapeutically approved drugs, several compounds originated from natural products are metabolized by the gut microbiota.

Many natural products contain glycosylated components prone to deglycosylation by microbiota within the intestine, producing more absorbable forms (Park 2019; Zhang et al. Reduction and hydrolysis reactions have also been observed with natural compounds depending on their structures.

Direct metabolism by the gut microbiota has been suggested for baicalin, berberine, ginsenoside Rb1, and glycyrrhizin after incubation with human feces or cecal contents isolated from animals (Akao et al. 1998; Kim et al. 2000; Trinh et al. 2010; Feng et al. The biological effects of natural products are sometimes exerted by metabolites produced by the activity of gut microbiota, and in vitro and in vivo efficacy studies may show different results, leading to inconsistent conclusions.
Hence, understanding the metabolic processes of natural compounds by gut microbiota will be helpful for the interpretation of the results and guide the direction of further research.

Gut microbiota alters expression of host drug‑metabolizing enzymes Various studies have suggested that the gut microbiota contributes to alterations in host drug-metabolizing enzyme expressions (Haiser and Turnbaugh 2013; Sun et al. 2019; Flowers et al. Because drug metabolism is one of the pivotal components determining the pharmacokinetic properties of many drugs, altered expression of host drugmetabolizing enzymes by the gut microbiota may change pharmacokinetic profiles and subsequently affect the efficacy or toxicity of the drugs.
This can explain one of the indirect mechanisms by which the gut microbiota affects drug metabolism.
Host drug metabolism is dominated by the cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme systems, with approximately 50% of drugs being metabolized through this enzyme system (Di 20.

In previous studies, alterations in the expression of several Cyp isozymes have occurred in germ-free (GF) mice which exhibit abacterial conditions (Table 2). (2009b) demonstrated that the mRNA expression levels of major Cyp isozymes, including Cyp1a2, 2b9, 2b13, 3a11, and 3a13, significantly decreased in the liver of GF mice and decreased protein level and activity of Cyp3a were also observed.

The decreased expression of Cyp3a in the livers of GF mice has also been reported in other several studies, confirming that the absence of microbiota is closely related to the decreased expression of Cyp3a (Xie et al. 2003; Kuno et al. 2016; Jourová et al. In contrast, increased expression of some Cyp isozymes, such as Cyp2a5, 2b13, 2c39, and 2c40, in the liver of GF mice has been reported, indicating the complex relationships between microbiota and Cyp expression.

In addition, contrary results on identical Cyp isozymes (e.g., Cyp2a4, 2c have been published, demanding a more careful approach for interpreting the research results (Toda et al. 2009b; Björkholm et al. 2009; Selwyn et al. 2015; Jourová et al. Another strategy to evaluate the role of microbiota in expressional changes in CYP is to use antibiotics to diminish the gut microbiota.

Administration of ciprofloxacin to reduce microbiota for the short term in mice decreased the mRNA levels of Cyp2c11, Cyp3a1, and Cyp3a11 in the liver, with a significant increase in systemic exposure to cyclophosphamide, which is metabolized by these Cyp isozymes (Xie et al. 2003; Toda et al. In addition, treatment with vancomycin and polymyxin B decreased the protein levels of Cyp2b10, Cyp3a11, and Cyp3a25 and increased the protein level of Cyp51a1 in the liver.

In another study, colonization of Lactobacillus plantarumNIZO2877 or probiotic bacteria Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 in GF mice altered the levels of Cyp1a2 and 2e1 in the liver (Jourová et al. It has been reported that microbiota also affects other phase I enzymes besides the CYP family.

Kuno et al. (20 and Selwyn et al. (20 revealed that the expression levels of aldo-keto reductase (AKR), aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH), aldehyde oxidase (AO), flavin-containing monooxygenase (FMO), and carboxylesterases (CE) were lower in GF mice than in specific-pathogen free mice.
In addition, the expression of phase II enzymes catalyzing conjugation reactions can be affected by the microbiota.

For example, some members of glutathione-S-transferase (GST), sulfotransferases (SULT), and uridine 5’-diphosphophate (UDP)glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) showed altered expression in GF mice or Caco-2 cells treated with colonic metabolites (González-Sarrías et al. 2015; Kuno et al. However, these investigations mostly showed mRNA level alterations; thus, alterations in protein expression and consequential functional changes by gut microbiota need to be evaluated further to estimate its clinical impact.

The mechanisms by which the gut microbiota affects the expression of drug-metabolizing enzymes have not yet been fully elucidated; however, the involvement of nuclear receptors has been the most frequently suggested mechanism (Tolson and Wang 20.

Nuclear receptors consist of a DNA-binding domain that links them to the promoter regions of their target genes and a ligand-binding domain that enables them to communicate with ligands directly and regulate the transcription of genes that contribute to a wide variety of biological pathways such as cell proliferation, differentiation, and reproduction (Evans 1988; Bourguet et al. Some of these nuclear receptors, including the constitutive androstane receptor (CAR), pregnane X receptor (PXR), farnesoid X receptor (FXR), liver X receptor, vitamin D receptor (VDR), and aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), regulate drug-metabolizing enzymes (Tolson and Wang 2010; Wu et al. 2012; Watanabe et al. 2013; Choi et al. If metabolites formed by gut microbiota activate or repress these nuclear receptors by acting on their ligands or stabilizing the nuclear receptors, this may cause alterations in the expression of metabolizing enzymes, resulting in pharmacokinetic variations of drugs.

A representative example of gut microbiota-derived metabolites that regulate the expression of drug-metabolizing enzymes is lithocholic acid produced by microbiota, such as Bacteroides, Lactobacillus, Clostridium, and Bifidobacterium from chenodeoxycholic acid, and is reported to activate nuclear receptors including FXR, PXR, and CAR (Wang et al. 1999; Staudinger et al. Decreased Cyp3a11 expression was observed in antibiotic-treated mice along with a decrease in lithocholic acid, suggesting the potential contribution of microbial metabolites to drug metabolism by altering the expression of metabolizing enzymes (Toda et al. Indole 3-propionic acid (IPA), a deaminated metabolite of tryptophan formed by the gut microbiota, is another example of this mechanism, which can activate PXR, thereby increasing the expression of target genes such as CYP3A (Venkatesh et al. 2014; Dodd et al. 2017; Wikoff et al. 20 observed that mice exposed to Clostridium sporogenes, which converts tryptophan into IPA, presented significant induction of Cyp3a11 in the intestine, experimentally demonstrating the crucial roles of gut microbiota in the regulation of drugmetabolizing enzyme expression (Venkatesh et al. Recent experiments have shown that microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) such as butyrate help stabilize the AhR, thus enhancing the expression of its target genes, including Cyp1a1, in response to ligands (Jin et al. However, information on the roles of microbiota in Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 53:73–92 the expression of drug-metabolizing enzymes is still quite limited; thus, more studies need to be focused on their relationship to explain this mechanism clearly.

The gut microbiota may contribute to the altered expression of metabolizing enzymes in the disease state, although there is a limitation to clear explanations for the relevance at present because of the limited information available.

Variations in the gut microbiota in disease states have been observed in many diseases, such as Parkinson’s disease, IBD, or diabetes (Zheng et al. 2018; Khan et al. 2019; Jin et al. When supernatant of colon contents from diabetic rats was treated into Caco-2 cells, decreased expression of CYP3A was observed, implying that the altered composition of microbial products in diabetes regulates the expression of drug-metabolizing enzymes with the potential to change the pharmacokinetic profiles of drugs (Hu et al. Further investigations are required to better understand the relevance of gut microbiota to drug-metabolizing enzymes.

Significant effects on intestinal metabolism have been reported for several drugs such as midazolam, cyclosporine, and nifedipine (Wu et al. 1995; Thummel et al. 1996; Holtbecker et al. 19, and the intestine is the tissue most closely located to the gut microbiota and their products.
However, most studies on the association of the gut microbiome with drug metabolism have focused on the liver.

Drugs with significant first-pass metabolism in the intestine tend to show high inter-individual pharmacokinetic variability, and the gut microbiota vulnerable to diet, age, or disease states may contribute to this variability.
Accordingly, more research needs to be focused on alterations in the expression of drug-metabolizing enzymes in the intestine by gut microbiota.

Microbial metabolites competitively inhibit host drug‑metabolizing enzymes A wide range of knowledge and information has become available on gut microbiota; accordingly, microbiota-associated metabolites have been focused on their various roles in the host.
In addition to the roles in regulating expression of drug-metabolizing enzymes reviewed above, microbial metabolites produced by gut microbiota can compete with drugs for drug-metabolizing enzymes.
When drugs compete with microbial metabolites for drug-metabolizing enzymes, unexpectedly altered drug concentrations may change drug efficacy, eventually resulting in treatment failure.
Acetaminophen is a representative example of competitive inhibition of host drug-metabolizing enzymes with microbial metabolites.
There are two main metabolism pathway with acetaminophen: glucuronidation by UGT and sulfation by SULT (McGill and Jaeschke 20.

Only a small amount of acetaminophen is converted into Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 53:73–92 N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), a hepatotoxic compound, by CYP1A2, 2E1, and 3A4 when the capacity of the conjugating enzymes is not saturated.
The small amount of NAPQI formed within the body can usually be detoxified by glutathione (GSH), which protects the liver.

However, when GSH is depleted for several reasons, such as alcohol consumption, or excess NAPQI is over the capacity of conjugation, NAPQI induces hepatotoxicity by attacking the thiol groups of proteins, subsequently inducing adduct formation.
Thus, a well-balanced metabolism of acetaminophen is important to avoid severe acute liver damage.

P-cresol, the metabolite of tyrosine and phenylalanine produced by the gut microbiota, is a substrate of SULT (Saito et al. The capacity of SULT is limited in humans; therefore, p-cresol can compete with acetaminophen to promote other metabolic processes such as the formation of NAPQI.
This competition eventually increases the concentration of NAPQI, thereby inducing hepatotoxicity.
Clayton et al. (20 observed that individuals with high pre-dose p-cresol sulfate levels in urine showed a low post-dose ratio of acetaminophen sulfate/ glucuronide.
Thus, individuals with high p-cresol concentrations may be more vulnerable to acetaminopheninduced liver toxicity.

Because acetaminophen has become the most common cause of acute liver failure in the United States (Lee 20, impact for intake of food containing high amount of tyrosine and phenylalanine, or environmental or pathophysiological factors changing excretion of p-cresol by gut microbiota, such as Clostridium difficile need to be investigated to reduce unexpected acetaminophen-induced liver toxicity (Saito et al. Quercetin is a flavonoid abundant in daily foods and dietary supplements and has various pharmacological activities such as anticancer, antioxidant, and neuroprotective effects (Zou et al. Diverse quercetin metabolites have been reported to be formed by the gut microbiota after oral administration (Di Pede et al. 20, and some of these metabolites have inhibitory potency against xanthine oxidase.

In particular, sulfateand methyl-conjugated metabolites of quercetin showed a 10-fold stronger inhibitory effect on 6-mercaptopurine oxidation than allopurinol, a well-known xanthine oxidase inhibitor with the potential to cause toxicity when co-administered with 6-mercaptopurine by increasing systemic exposure (Mohos et al. Therefore, a high intake of quercetin with drugs metabolized by xanthine oxidase may induce fatal outcomes due to altered pharmacokinetics.
Another example of competitive inhibition of host drug metabolism by microbial metabolites is the interaction between sorivudine and 5-fluorouracil (5-FU).
Sorivudine, a nucleoside analog antiviral drug used to treat varicellazoster virus infection, produces bromovinyluracil via the gut microbiota, such as Bacteroidetes sp. or Klebsiella pneumoniae.

This metabolite takes over dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) in an irreversible manner, reducing functionally active DPD (Yan et al. When sorivudine is concomitantly administered with 5-FU, the drug metabolized by DPD, toxic effects can be induced by the inhibition of 5-FU metabolism and consequent accumulation of 5-FU. Fatal events induced by this interaction were reported in 23 cases of severe toxicity, including 16 patients who eventually died, and these cases created close attention to the interactions between microbial metabolites and host drugmetabolizing enzymes (Diasio 19.
Several natural products used as dietary supplements are glycosylated forms, which are prone to be deglycosylated by gut microbiota.

Roles of gut microbiota becomes important if deglycosylated products competitively inhibit drug metabolizing enzymes of host, while glycosylated forms do not present inhibitory effect son the enzymes.
For example, the majority of ginsenoside, which are the main components of ginseng, are deglycosylated by gut microbiota producing aglycones such as 20(S)-protopanaxadiol and 20(S)protopanaxatriol.
Liu et al. (20 demonstrated 20(S)protopanaxadiol and 20(S)-protopanaxatriol have strong CYP3A4 inhibitory potency while their glycosylated forms are unlikely to inhibit CYP3A4.

In the study by Lee et al. (20, in vivo interaction potential of 20(S)-protopanaxadiol by CYP3A4 inhibition has been proven, highlighting the importance of gut microbiota-mediated metabolism in drug interactions.
However, only a few publications have reported on the competition with microbial metabolites compared to the other mechanisms.
Further study on this field is warranted so as to develop an optimal therapy strategy considering this mechanism.

Altered drug transport by gut microbiota More than 400 membrane transporters have been identified in the human genome, belonging to the solute carrier (SLC) and ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter superfamilies.
Transporters are involved in absorption, distribution, and excretion processes of drugs.

Altered functions of drug transporters may change the pharmacokinetic profiles of drugs, consequently affecting efficacy or safety (Chae et al. 2021a; Zheng et al. Mechanisms for the altered function of drug transporters by the gut microbiota can be divided into expressional changes and competitive inhibition by microbial metabolites (Fig. Although the information on the relationship between transporters and gut microbiota is much less than that on drug-metabolizing enzymes, the importance of this relationship should not be overlooked considering the contribution of transporters to drug pharmacokinetics.

Gut microbiota alters expression of host drug transporters Various nuclear receptors such as PXR, CAR, and FXR contribute to the regulation of drug transporters (Tirona 2011; Balla et al. Similar to the mechanisms reviewed in sections for the drug-metabolizing enzyme above, microbial metabolites can activate or repress the nuclear receptors regulating drug transporters, altering substrate drug pharmacokinetics (Table 3).
Efflux transporters pump substrate drugs out of the cells, leading to decreased bioavailability or increased drug excretion in most cases.

Multidrug resistance protein 1 (MDR and multidrug resistance-associated protein 2 (MRP are important efflux transporters expressed in various tissues, such as the intestine, liver, brain, and kidney.

Downregulation of MDR1 and MRP2 was observed in Caco-2 cells treated with Lactobacillus murinus (Yuan et al. 20, whereas Lactobacillus acidophilus or Lactobacillus rhamnosus culture supernatant induced the upregulation of MDR1.

The factors contributing to the altered expression remain unknown, but these kinds of studies investigating specific microbiota types can provide more detailed information to correlate their relationships.
The expression of uptake transporters, which play important roles in the movement of drugs into cells, was also suggested to be modulated by the gut microbiota.

GF mice showed lower expression of apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporters (Asbt), organic anion transporting polypeptide 1b2 (Oatp1b, and organic cation transporter (Oct than normal mice (Selwyn et al. Although a few investigations on transporter expression have been performed in relation to gut microbiota to date, more investigations on their relationship are expected to increase, as interest in transporters in drug pharmacokinetics increases.

Microbial metabolites competitively inhibit host drug transporters Metabolites produced by the gut microbiota may competitively inhibit drug transporters expressed in tissues, altering drug absorption, disposition, and excretion.
Metabolites may be produced from endogenous compounds such as bile acid, drugs, or any diet including dietary supplements, by the gut microbiota.

González-Sarrías et al. (20 observed that urolithin A, produced by gut microbiota from ellagic acid, inhibits transport of mitoxantrone, which is a sensitive BCRP substrate, in a dose-dependent manner, suggesting that the intake of ellagic acid can modulate the transport of BCRP substrate drugs mediated by competitive inhibition.
Because many anticancer drugs are substrates of efflux transporters, such as BCRP, the activity of gut microbiota may be associated with the extent of drug resistance in some cases.

Most statins are substrates of OATP transporters, such as OATP1B1, and co-administration of inhibitors of OATP transporters induces an elevation in plasma concentrations of statins, resulting in life-threatening muscle toxicity called rhabdomyolysis (Balasubramanian and Maideen 20.

In a recent study, deoxycholic acid, a metabolite of cholic acid produced by the gut microbiota, was reported to be transported by OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 (Suga et al. Accordingly, deoxycholic acid may compete with statins for OATP transporters, subsequently altering the pharmacokinetic profiles of statins.

Other mechanisms altering drug pharmacokinetics Altered tight junction by gut microbiota The intestinal mucosal barrier consists of epithelial cells with tight junctions, immune cells that prevent the transmission of pathogens, and a mucosal layer that harbors the gut microbiota.
The microbiota can affect xenobiotic absorption in various ways, including modifying intestinal permeability by modulating tight junctions or thickening the intestinal mucus layer.

In an early study by Hughes et al. (20, increased paracellular permeability was observed in vitro following treatment with secondary bile acids, such as lithocholic acid or deoxycholic acid, produced by gut microbial metabolites.
In contrast, primary bile acids, including cholic acid or chenodeoxycholic acid, did not alter paracellular permeability.
Based on this study, it seems plausible that the gut microbiota modulate tight junctions, altering epithelial barrier function.
In addition to the in vitro study, associations between gut microbiota and tight junctions have been reported in an in vivo study.

It has been reported that tight junction proteins, such as claudin-7, occludin, and zonula occludens (ZO)-1, are lower in GF mice than in normal mice (Shimada et al. Along with this finding, the concentration of indole, a metabolite of tryptophan by tryptophanase activity of gut microbiota, decreased markedly in the feces of GF mice by 27-fold, and administration of indole into GF mice for 2 weeks resulted in increased expression of tight junction proteins, as well as reduced weight loss in mice with dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-induced colitis, which is a model of IBD associated with disrupted tight junctions in intestinal epithelial cells.

Another research team observed that administration of antibiotic cocktails to mice induced an increase in intestinal permeability of fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)-dextran, which is a marker of paracellular transport and decreased expression of tight junction proteins (Feng et al. The exact mechanism remains unknown; however, SCFAs, important for the intestinal barrier derived from gut microbiota, decreased accompanied by alterations in microbiota composition.
These results suggest that the gut microbiota is involved in intestinal tight junction formation potentially by modulating tight junction protein expression using microbial metabolites.

As drug permeability across the intestinal barrier significantly contributes to their pharmacokinetic profiles, altered tight junctions between intestinal epithelial cells by gut microbiota may lead to changes in drug pharmacokinetic changes.

Several investigations have suggested a possible relationship between gut microbial dysbiosis observed under pathophysiological conditions and alterations in tight junctions in the intestinal barrier.

Increased intestinal permeability under obesity, high-fat diet-fed insulin resistance, or chronic kidney disease is accompanied by profound alterations of gut microbiota, although the mechanisms are still uncertain (Lau and Vaziri 2017; Nagpal et al. 2018; Chen et al. Adsorption of drugs with gut microbiota It seems evident that the presence of Helicobacter pylori is associated with decreased systemic exposure to L-dopa, the first approved drug for treating Parkinson’s disease in humans.

Several reports on the decreased L-dopa concentration in Parkinson’s patients infected with H. pylori and the increased L-dopa concentration within the body after eradicating H. pylori support this association (Pierantozzi et al. 2006; Nyholm and Hellström 20.

Altered exposure to L-dopa also induced modification of treatment efficacy, suggesting that H. pylori plays a substantial role in treating Parkinson’s disease (Hashim et al. 2014; Lolekha et al. The adhesion of L-dopa to H. pylori is one of plausible mechanisms for the relationship.

Niehues and Hensel (20 observed that the concentration of unbound L-dopa significantly decreased when incubated with H. pylori in vitro in a time-and concentration-dependent manner, along with a decrease in bacterial adhesion to gastric epithelial cells.
Another potential adsorption case has been reported for SN-38, the active metabolite of irinotecan.

In a clinical study of small cell lung cancer patients, more than 15% of patients taking irinotecan experienced grade 3/4 diarrhea with early or late-onset (Noda et al. When SN-38 was incubated with cecal contents isolated from rats, free SN-38 in the supernatant decreased rapidly and reached a plateau within 1 h, which remained for up to 24 h, while a decrease in irinotecan was not observed.

This research suggests that SN-38 may bind to hydrophobic bacterial cell walls owing to the hydrophobic and lipophilic properties of SN-38, which may explain late-onset diarrhea observed in patients taking irinotecan (Yamamoto et al. However, the mechanisms Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 53:73–92 or factors contributing to the binding between bacteria and drugs remain unclear.

Limitations of current research and perspectives of future directions Considering the critical roles of gut microbiota in drug pharmacokinetics and drug efficacy, suggestions to apply information on gut microbiota in individualized therapy have been increasing (Rajpoot et al. 2018; Schupack et al. Although prominent advances in research have paved the way to link gut microbiota and drug pharmacokinetics, there are still some limitations and restrictions to understanding their intricate association.
A widely used model for studying gut microbiota is the GF animal model.
The idea of GF animals was first suggested in 1885 and GF mice were successfully developed in 1959 (Pleasants 19.
The use of GF animals has expanded our knowledge of the gut microbiota in association with disease, the immune system, and drug pharmacokinetics.
In addition, GF models can be utilized to generate gnotobiotic models colonized with the bacteria of interest to investigate the definite roles of the specified bacterial strain.
However, GF animals differ from normal mice not only in the existence of bacteria but also in other physiological conditions.

For example, GF mice are more susceptible to infection because of severely defective immune systems (Deplancke and Gaskins 20 and exhibit altered behaviors and responses to stress caused by reduced levels of neurotransmitters such as dopamine or serotonin (Borre et al. These differences can be attributed to the presence of microbiota; however, they may act as confounding factors in studying the mechanisms of the relationship between microbiota and drug pharmacokinetics.
In addition, specialized facilities and intensive care are necessary to maintain GF conditions, restricting the wider use of GF animals.

As an alternative method, antibiotic-treated models have been applied to the study of gut microbiota; however, it is necessary to clarify whether the observed results are caused by the altered status of microbiota or the interactions of antibiotics and drugs via different pathways.
Thus, particular attention should be paid to studies using GF- or antibiotic-treated animals to determine the associations between gut microbiota and drug pharmacokinetics.
Technical limitations may also hamper advances in research on the microbiota.
Elucidation of the bacterial strains involved in alterations of drug pharmacokinetics is essential to expand the information on further research for clinical applications.

Sequencing of 16S rDNA, which is a component of the ribosome 30S subunit in bacteria, is widely used to identify and quantify microbiota in complex mixtures, such as gut samples (Hold et al. However, Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 53:73–92 the 16S rDNA sequencing method has limitations in providing accurate discrimination of some bacteria within the same family, producing uncertain information (Woo et al. Instead, metagenomics or metabolomics are becoming conjunct with microbial research alongside the progress of the “-omics” era. Due to the complexity and diversity of the microbiome and its metabolites, metagenomic or metabolomic techniques are suitable for investigating novel functional genes or functional dysbiosis of the microbiota or microbial pathways (Wang et al. 2015; Chen et al. Despite the high cost and requirement for massive amounts of information for analysis, the expanded use of -omics techniques is expected to further improve the accuracy and efficiency of microbial investigations.
Still, most research on gut microbiota is confined to in vitro or pre-clinical animal studies.
A few clinical results reported to date have not clarified their underlying mechanisms because of the lack of studies at the molecular level.

Translational research integrating clinical studies and in vitro/pre-clinical studies may provide a revolutionary approach to provide crucial information on the gut microbiota and ultimately advance microbiome-based personalized therapy.
Application of physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling method can be one of the tools to incorporate knowledge obtained in vitro and in vivo.

Zimmermann et al. (20 quantified microbial contribution to systemic metabolite levels by developing PBPK model and simulated the effect of microbiota on the systemic exposures to drugs and metabolites under various conditions including altered microbiota enzyme activity.
This approach will aid in minimizing risk of treatment failure by providing quantitative approach in understanding roles of microbiota in drug pharmacokinetics.
Conclusion Understanding the gut microbiota is expected to be a continuous subject of interest in investigations to improve human health.
Gut microbiota can alter drug pharmacokinetics by affecting drug metabolizing enzymes and transporters, which are major contributing factors in pharmacokinetics.

Representative mechanisms on these associations include direct metabolism by gut microbiota using their metabolizing activity, modulation of the relevant genes, competitive inhibition by their metabolites, or other mechanisms.
Investigations into the roles of the gut microbiota in drug pharmacokinetics are crucial for optimizing therapy to meet the intended treatment goal.

Although substantial advances in research have linked gut microbiota and drug pharmacokinetics in part, there are still some restrictions to fully understand their intricate association and underlying mechanisms.
Particular attention should be paid to studies using germ-free or antibiotic-treated animals owing to several confounding factors.

Technical limitations may also impede advances in research on microbiota, and the expanded use of -omics techniques is expected to further improve the accuracy and efficiency of microbial investigations.

Most research on gut microbiota is confined to in vitro or pre-clinical animal studies at present, and further application of translational research integrating clinical studies and in vitro/pre-clinical studies is warranted to provide information on associations between the gut microbiota and drug pharmacokinetics.
Expanded information on roles of gut microbiota in drug pharmacokinetics will facilitate microbiome-based personalized therapy.
